sections.text: ## Why Pigments Degrade

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: ### Photodegradation (Organic Pigments)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
MECHANISM:
  UV light (300-400 nm) absorbed by organic chromophore
  -> Electronic excitation (S0 -> S1 or Sn)
  -> Photochemical reactions:
    Homolytic bond cleavage -> radical chain reactions
    Oxidation of conjugated π system
    Hydrolysis in presence of moisture

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
RATE FACTORS:
  UV intensity: direct sun > window light > museum (filtered)
  Humidity: moisture accelerates hydrolysis
  Oxygen: required for oxidative pathways
  Temperature: Arrhenius dependence - higher T = faster

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
TYPICAL VULNERABLE CHROMOPHORES:
  Azo dyes (−N=N−): direct UV cleavage
  Anthraquinones (alizarin): moderately stable, eventually fades
  Indigotin: relatively stable for organic (ASTM II typically)
  Flavonoids (weld, quercitron): generally ASTM III-IV
  Rhodamines (fluorescent): very fast degradation (ASTM V)
```

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: ### Inorganic Pigment Degradation

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
MECHANISMS (varied):

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
1. VALENCE STATE CHANGE:
   Chrome yellow (Cr⁶⁺ -> Cr³⁺): photoreduction
   Smalt (Co²⁺ leaches from glass): slow dissolution
   Prussian blue (partial): some conditions -> Turnbull's blue (different form)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
2. SULFIDATION:
   Lead . H₂S -> PbS (black)
   Silver . H₂S -> Ag₂S (black)
   Copper -> CuS (black) [less common]
   H₂S source: biological activity, industrial pollution, some materials

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
3. CONVERSION:
   Azurite (Cu carbonate blue) -> malachite (Cu carbonate green)
   Thermodynamically driven, irreversible
   Triggered by: moisture + CO₂

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
4. MIGRATION:
   Smalt: Co²⁺ migrates in oil -> staining of surrounding area
   Lead soap: Pb²⁺ migrates in oil -> zinc soap forms with ZnO
   Protrusion formation: soap crystals grow through surface

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
5. PHOTOREDUCTION (semiconductor pigments):
   PbCrO₄ -> Cr³⁺ green compounds
   CdS -> partial reduction under UV (minor in normal conditions)
```

sections.text: ### Blue Wool Scale (ISO 105-B02)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
BLUE WOOL SCALE:
  Eight wool samples (1-8) dyed with known lightfast-to-fugitive range:
  1 = most fugitive; 8 = most lightfast (indanthrone blue standard)
  Comparison standard in textile industry
  Also used for watercolor/artist materials in EU

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
CORRELATION to ASTM:
  Blue Wool 7-8 ≈ ASTM I
  Blue Wool 5-6 ≈ ASTM II
  Blue Wool 3-4 ≈ ASTM III
  (Approximate mapping; test conditions differ)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
TEST PROCEDURE:
  Cover half the sample with opaque mask
  Expose exposed half to specified light source for specified time
  Remove mask; compare covered vs exposed areas against Blue Wool standards
  Repeat at intervals -> determine Blue Wool rating when change equals BW1
```

sections.text: ## Notable Color Changes in Famous Works

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
VAN GOGH'S SUNFLOWERS (multiple versions, 1888):
  Chrome yellow (PbCrO₄) -> Cr⁶⁺ photoreduced to Cr³⁺
  Result: yellow -> brown-green in affected areas
  Detection: synchrotron XRF maps showing Cr distribution
  "Virtual restoration": simulated original based on spectral data
  The bright yellow fields van Gogh intended ≠ what we see

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
VERMEER'S "WOMAN IN BLUE READING A LETTER" (~1663-64):
  Blue areas: mix of natural ultramarine + smalt
  Smalt = unstable cobalt glass -> Co leaches -> color fades to gray
  Current appearance: grayish-blue vs original deep blue
  The painting is darker/grayer than painted

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
RAPHAEL'S "MADONNA OF THE GOLDFINCH" (c. 1505-06):
  Lead white . H₂S from Florentine urban atmosphere -> PbS darkening
  Major restoration history: damaged in 1547 when a flood and partial wall collapse
  struck the Uffizi; survived; subsequent cleanings and interventions over centuries;
  most recent major restoration ~2008 using H₂O₂ vapor treatment
  H₂O₂ vapor treatment -> PbS -> PbSO₄ (white)
  Brightening documented and remarkable

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
RENOIR'S FLESH TONES (throughout career):
  Lake-heavy pinks -> photodegradation of organic chromophore
  Original vivid pinks -> current muted pink-salmon
  "The Renoir look" partly = what decay looks like, not what he painted

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
REMBRANDT'S NIGHT WATCH (1642):
  Smalt areas in sky/background -> faded gray
  The dark "Night Watch" was originally lighter
  Title "Night Watch" = 19th century misnomer based on darkened appearance
  Original: a daytime scene with lighter background

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
EL GRECO FLESH TONES:
  Lead white . smalt mixtures -> smalt graying . lead soap transparency
  Complex interaction -> distinctive grayish-pink translucency
  Partly original technique; partly 400 years of change
```

sections.text: ## Analytical Methods for Conservation

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: ### X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
XRF PRINCIPLE:
  X-rays bombard sample -> inner-shell electrons ejected
  -> Outer electrons fall inward -> characteristic fluorescence X-rays emitted
  Each element has unique fluorescence energy (Moseley's Law)
  -> Non-destructive elemental analysis

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
PIGMENT IDENTIFICATION:
  Pb (lead white, red lead, Naples yellow, chrome yellow)
  Hg (vermilion/cinnabar)
  As (orpiment, realgar, emerald green)
  Cu (malachite, azurite, verdigris, Egyptian blue)
  Cd (cadmium yellow/red)
  Co (cobalt blue, smalt)
  Cr (chrome yellow, viridian)
  Ti (titanium white - post 1916)
  Sb (Naples yellow)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
MA-XRF (Macro Area X-ray Fluorescence):
  Full painting scanned in 2D -> element distribution maps
  Shows: where each pigment was applied
         Underpaintings (lead white under oil shows through)
         Changes/corrections (different element distribution beneath surface)
         Artist's palette mapped spatially

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
NON-DESTRUCTIVE: No sampling required; museum-approved
```

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: ### Raman Spectroscopy

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
RAMAN PRINCIPLE:
  Laser light inelastically scattered from molecular vibrations
  Each molecule has unique vibrational fingerprint
  -> Identifies specific compounds, not just elements

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
ADVANTAGE OVER XRF:
  XRF: "lead is present"
  Raman: "the lead compound is cerussite specifically, not hydrocerussite"
         "this is malachite, not azurite" (both = Cu; Raman distinguishes)
         "this is Egyptian blue, not Han blue"

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
COMPOUND-LEVEL IDENTIFICATION:
  Distinguishes: calcite/aragonite, malachite/azurite, hematite/goethite
  Can identify: lapis lazuli lazurite, Prussian blue, synthetic ultramarine
  Detection of: titanium white polymorph (anatase vs rutile)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
PORTABLE INSTRUMENTS:
  Handheld Raman spectrometers (2010s development)
  In-gallery analysis without moving works
  "Point-and-shoot" identification
  Limitation: fluorescence can mask Raman signal (organic materials)
```

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: ### Infrared Reflectography (IRR)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
IRR PRINCIPLE:
  Near-infrared light (1,000-2,000 nm) penetrates oil paint layers
  Carbon-based materials absorb IR strongly (charcoal, carbon-based inks)
  -> Underdrawing visible through paint layers

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
REVEALS:
  Initial underdrawing: black chalk, charcoal, carbon ink, ink drawings
  Compositional changes: artist repositioned figures, objects
  Pentimento: earlier rejected compositions
  Grid lines: preparatory transfer grids
  Authentication evidence: drawing style matches/doesn't match artist

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
FAMOUS EXAMPLES:
  Raphael's Sistine Madonna: complex underdrawing revealed
  Vermeer works: limited underdrawing (works directly from life or camera obscura)
  Van Eyck's Ghent Altarpiece: detailed underdrawing, some areas modified

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
LIMITATION:
  Only reveals CARBON-BASED drawing materials
  Metal-point drawings, red chalk, colored ground: not always visible
```

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: ### UV Fluorescence

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
UV FLUORESCENCE (UV-VIS reflectography):
  Short-wave UV (254 nm, "black light") illuminates painting
  Various materials fluoresce differently under UV:

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
FLUORESCENCE PATTERNS:
  Old varnish (oxidized): yellow-green fluorescence
  Modern varnish (synthetic, fresh): blue-white
  Egg tempera: strong white-green
  Oil paint (aged): pale green or dark (quench areas)
  Restoration patches: often very different from surroundings
    -> Patches glow or go dark against overall surface
  Lead white: fluoresces differently than surrounding areas
  Egyptian blue: NIR fluorescence (requires NIR camera, not visible UV)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
CONSERVATION USE:
  Mapping of previous restorations (patches visible)
  Varnish distribution uniformity
  Identifying later additions
```

sections.text: ## Forensic Authentication — Pigment Anachronism

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: The most powerful forgery detection method: if a painting contains a pigment that didn't exist at its claimed date, it's a forgery.

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
CHRONOLOGICAL CONSTRAINTS:
.------------------.----------------------------------------.
| Pigment          | Earliest possible date in work         |
.------------------.----------------------------------------.
| Prussian blue    | 1704 (accidental discovery, Berlin)   |
| Synthetic ultra  | 1826 (Guimet + Gmelin)                |
| Chrome yellow    | ~1814 (commercial availability)       |
| Cobalt blue      | ~1802                                  |
| Zinc white       | ~1840 (commercial)                    |
| Cadmium yellow   | ~1848 (commercial)                    |
| Viridian         | ~1838                                  |
| Alizarin crimson | 1869 (Perkin/Graebe-Liebermann)       |
| Emerald green    | ~1814 (Schweinfurt)                   |
| Titanium white   | 1916 (commercial)                     |
| Phthalocyanine   | 1935 (commercial)                     |
| Quinacridone     | 1958 (commercial)                     |
.------------------.----------------------------------------.

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
IF: Titanium white in "17th century Vermeer" -> FORGERY
IF: Phthalocyanine in "Rembrandt" -> FORGERY
IF: Prussian blue in "1600 Italian work" -> FORGERY
```

sections.text: ### Famous Forgeries Detected by Pigment Analysis

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
HANS VAN MEEGEREN (1889-1947):
  Dutch forger of "Vermeer" and other Dutch Masters
  His "Supper at Emmaus" sold for 520,000 guilders (1937)
  Eventually confessed (to avoid WWII collaboration charges)

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
DETECTION METHOD:
  Bakelite found in paint medium (phenol-formaldehyde resin)
  Bakelite: invented 1907 - cannot be present in 17th century work
  Also: cobaltic blue used where Vermeer wouldn't have had it
  The specific material anachronism caught what stylistic analysis missed

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
ELMYR DE HORY (1906-1976):
  Most prolific 20th century art forger
  Forged: Matisse, Picasso, Renoir, Modigliani (~1,000 works)
  Detection: partly via technical analysis
  Issue: used modern "student grade" materials with synthetic components
  absent from genuine works of claimed period

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis
Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
MARK LANDIS (born 1955):
  American forger who donated works to museums (not for sale)
  Claimed to be his deceased sister's paintings or family heirlooms
  Donated to 50+ museums over 30 years
  Detection: systematic comparison of donations by Matthew Leininger
  Scientific analysis found: modern acrylic binders, commercial paper
  inconsistent with claimed dates/origins
```

sections.text: ## Original Polychrome: The White Marble Myth

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
THE NEOCLASSICAL MISUNDERSTANDING:
  When Renaissance and later scholars/artists excavated Greek/Roman
  sculpture, they found WHITE marble (paint had weathered off)
  -> Assumed: ancient sculpture = white marble aesthetic
  -> This aesthetic dominated Neoclassicism (Canova, Thorvaldsen)
  -> The "purity" of white marble = idealized classical body

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
THE REALITY:
  Ancient Greek and Roman sculpture was PAINTED in vivid colors
  Physical evidence:
  1. UV fluorescence: paint residue glows on sculpture surfaces
  2. Microsampling: trace pigments in protected crevices
  3. Literary sources: ancient writers describe painted statues

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
PIGMENTS FOUND ON ANCIENT SCULPTURE:
  Egyptian blue (see 02-ANCIENT-SYNTHETIC.md): widely used
  Red ochre (hematite): flesh tones
  Yellow ochre: gilded-like areas
  Azurite: drapery blues
  Cinnabar: lips, features

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
FAMOUS EXAMPLES:
  Peplos Kore (Acropolis, Athens): detailed reconstruction shows
  vivid red/green/blue on marble surface
  Warrior from Riace: traces of original pigment
  Elgin Marbles: pigment traces visible under UV

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
"Gods in Color" project (Vinzenz Brinkmann):
  Comprehensive reconstruction of ancient polychrome sculpture
  Exhibition toured internationally; deeply unsettling to audiences
  raised on white marble aesthetic

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
IMPLICATION:
  The "timeless" aesthetic we associate with classical antiquity
  = an accident of 2,000 years of weathering misread as aesthetic intention
```

sections.text: ## Varnish Chemistry and Removal

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
```
TRADITIONAL VARNISHES:
  Mastic (resin from Pistacia lentiscus)
  Copal (fossilized/semi-fossil tree resin)
  Dammar (resin from Shorea trees)
  Applied as protective/glossy coat over finished painting

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
YELLOWING MECHANISM:
  Polyterpene and polyketo resins -> oxidative polymerization over decades
  Results: yellowed, darkened varnish layer
  Old master paintings viewed through yellow-brown filter
  This changes perceived color balance: blues suppressed, yellows enhanced

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
"GOLDEN GLAZE" myth: some 19th c. collectors valued the yellow patina
  as "old master atmosphere" - in fact, they were admiring dirty varnish

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
VARNISH REMOVAL:
  Organic solvent cleaning: dissolves varnish
  Risk: may also dissolve thin paint layers or sensitive pigments
  Must be tested in inconspicuous area first
  Specialist job - responsible for major museum controversies

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
NATIONAL GALLERY (London) cleaning controversy (1947-1953):
  Director Philip Hendy's cleaning policy revealed brighter Raphaels
  Critics argued originals were being damaged; supporters said restoring
  Original color balance; debate never fully resolved

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
MODERN SYNTHETIC VARNISHES:
  Paraloid B-72 (ethylene-methyl acrylate copolymer): extremely stable
  Laropal K80 (ketone resin): UV-stable, easily reversible
  "Conservation-grade" = reversible with known solvents = good practice
```

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text:
| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| What's the difference between ASTM I and II for an artist? | I = confident permanence for 100+ years in museum. II = acceptable for most purposes; some fade possible over 25 years. Use I for archival work. |
| How does XRF identify pigments? | Characteristic fluorescence X-rays emitted by inner-shell electrons — each element's emission energies are unique |
| How does Raman spectroscopy improve on XRF? | Identifies specific compounds (cerussite vs hydrocerussite; malachite vs azurite), not just elements |
| What does infrared reflectography reveal? | Carbon-based underdrawings under paint layers — compositional changes, preparatory work |
| How does pigment anachronism detect forgeries? | If a work contains a pigment that wasn't synthesized until after its claimed date, it cannot be authentic |
| What did Van Meegeren's forged Vermeers contain? | Bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde, invented 1907) in paint medium — physically impossible in 17th century work |
| Were ancient Greek/Roman sculptures white? | No — they were vigorously painted in vivid colors. The white marble "aesthetic" is 2,000 years of weathering misread as intention. |
| How is Prussian blue used medically? | FDA-approved antidote for Cs-137 and thallium poisoning — absorbs the ions in gut via ion exchange in its crystal lattice |

sections.text: ## Common Confusion Points

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: **"Cleaned" ≠ "damaged":** Removal of discolored varnish (often 1–2mm thick yellow layer) reveals original colors underneath. Some critics confuse varnish removal with removing paint. These are chemically distinct operations with different solvents and techniques.

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: **ASTM II is still useful:** "Not archival-grade" doesn't mean "it will fall apart." ASTM II = 25+ years in museum conditions. Most collectors' works are not in museum conditions. For personal use, ASTM II is often acceptable. For works intended to last generations, use ASTM I only.

metadata.title: Conservation and Authentication - Lightfastness, Forensic Pigment Analysis

sections.text: **Anachronism detection is definitive; stylistic analysis is not:** Pigment anachronism ("this has titanium white, so it can't be 1650") is chemical fact. Connoisseurship ("the brushwork doesn't feel like Rembrandt") is expert opinion. Major forgeries have survived stylistic review but failed chemical analysis. Science > expertise for this specific question.
